title: Straight-Line Motion: Position, Velocity, and Acceleration
subject: AP Calculus AB

chunks.text: For a particle moving along a line, position s(t) is its signed location, velocity is v(t) = s'(t), and acceleration is a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t).
Velocity is the derivative of position and acceleration is the derivative of velocity, so acceleration is the second derivative of position.
Velocity is signed: v(t) > 0 means the particle moves in the positive direction and v(t) < 0 means it moves in the negative direction.
When v(t) = 0 the particle is instantaneously at rest, and these are the only times it can change direction.
A particle changes direction at a time where v(t) = 0 only if v actually changes sign there; a velocity that touches zero without changing sign means a momentary pause, not a reversal.
Speed is the absolute value of velocity, |v(t)|, and is never negative; it measures how fast the particle moves regardless of direction.
Velocity and speed are different: a velocity of −8 has a higher speed than a velocity of −5, even though −8 is the smaller number.
A particle is speeding up when velocity and acceleration have the same sign, and slowing down when they have opposite signs.
Equivalently, a particle speeds up when the product v·a is positive and slows down when v·a is negative.
A negative acceleration does not by itself mean slowing down; a particle moving in the negative direction with negative acceleration is speeding up.
Driving analogy: moving forward and pressing the gas (same signs) speeds you up; moving forward and braking (opposite signs) slows you down.
To analyze motion, build sign charts of v(t) and a(t) on the time line, splitting at every zero of both, then read off direction and speeding-up behavior.
Example: for s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t, velocity is v(t) = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) and acceleration is a(t) = 6(t − 2).
For that particle, v = 0 at t = 1 and t = 3, where the particle is at rest and changes direction because v changes sign at each.
For that particle, the velocity is positive on (0,1), negative on (1,3), and positive on (3,∞), giving the direction of motion on each interval.
For that particle, comparing signs of v and a shows it speeds up on (1,2) and (3,4) and slows down on (0,1) and (2,3).
The zeros of acceleration correspond to inflection points of the position function, where the concavity of s(t) changes.
On free response, 'find the velocity' means differentiate position once and 'find the acceleration' means differentiate twice.
To justify whether speed is increasing, compare the signs of v and a at that instant rather than relying on a single value.
The rate of change of speed equals a when v > 0 and equals −a when v < 0, which is why speed increases exactly when a shares the sign of v.
Integrating velocity over an interval gives displacement (net change in position), a connection developed in the integration applications unit.
Integrating speed |v(t)| over an interval gives total distance traveled, which differs from displacement whenever the particle changes direction.
